title: Leg 53 — Craters of the Moon to Pocatello
subtitle: Lost River Valley, Arco, Craters of the Moon, Big Southern Butte and Pocatello
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. Today we're leaving Challis and heading southeast through the Lost River country toward Mackay and Arco, then crossing one of Idaho's strangest volcanic landscapes at Craters of the Moon. From there we'll continue across the eastern Snake River Plain past Big Southern Butte before turning toward Pocatello. Along the way we'll have mining history, the 1983 Borah Peak earthquake, atomic-age Idaho, lava fields, astronaut geology training, volcanic domes, emigrant trails, and the railroad city at the Portneuf Gap. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

waypoints.name: Craters North Viewing Pass
viewingNotes: Craters of the Moon lava fields remain off the right side of the west-southwestbound approach and then south of the eastbound departure track.

waypoints.name: Big Southern Butte East Pass
viewingNotes: Big Southern Butte sits off the right side during the eastbound pass across the volcanic plain.

blocks.title: Leaving the Challis Basin
blocks.text: Challis and the broad Salmon River basin are slipping behind us as we head southeast. The landscape ahead tightens again into long mountain ranges separated by high valleys. This part of Idaho belongs to Basin and Range country, where faults have repeatedly lifted mountain blocks and dropped the valleys between them.

blocks.title: The Lost River Range
blocks.text: The high wall building ahead and to the right is the Lost River Range. It contains Borah Peak, Idaho's highest summit at more than twelve thousand six hundred feet. The contrast between the straight valley floor and abrupt mountain front is not accidental; a major normal fault runs along the base of the range.

blocks.title: The earthquake that moved the mountains
blocks.text: On October twenty-eighth, 1983, a magnitude six point nine earthquake ruptured the Lost River fault. Parts of the mountain side rose while the valley side dropped, creating fresh fault scarps that could be measured for miles. Near Borah Peak, the range itself was lifted by roughly a foot relative to distant points.

blocks.title: A valley shaped by repeated faulting
blocks.text: That earthquake was dramatic, but geologists read it as one event in a much longer process. Repeated movements on faults like this are what built the Basin and Range topography around us: steep mountain fronts beside long, relatively flat valleys. From the air, the geometry is unusually easy to see.

blocks.title: A river that disappears
blocks.text: The Big Lost River drains this high valley but never reaches the Snake on the surface. After leaving the mountains it spreads onto the volcanic plain and sinks into gravel and fractured basalt. Much of that water eventually joins the great aquifer beneath eastern Idaho, linking this mountain valley to the volcanic country we will cross later.

blocks.title: Mining country ahead
blocks.text: As the valley opens farther south, we're approaching one of Idaho's important historic copper districts. The mountains around Mackay drew prospectors in the late nineteenth century, but serious development accelerated after richer copper discoveries and, later, the arrival of rail service.

blocks.title: White Knob and Idaho copper
blocks.text: The White Knob and Alder Creek mines above Mackay became major copper producers in the early twentieth century. For a time, the Mackay district and nearby Copper Basin together formed Idaho's leading copper-producing region. Old mine workings and tram routes still mark the slopes above the valley.

blocks.title: A railroad town created by mining
blocks.text: Mackay itself was founded in 1901 when the railroad reached the valley and a new mining center replaced smaller camps higher in the mountains. The town quickly grew around the ore traffic, smelter plans, shops and workers needed to support the mines.

blocks.title: Mackay in the valley
blocks.text: Mackay should be close now in the broad valley below. The town is small compared with the mountain wall beside it, which makes the old mining relationship easy to understand: settlement stayed on the flat ground while the mineral workings climbed into the rugged slopes above.

blocks.title: Down the Lost River Valley
blocks.text: South of Mackay, the route continues along the Lost River Valley. Despite the name, the Big Lost River does not ultimately reach the sea. Water from this basin sinks into the porous volcanic rocks of the Snake River Plain and continues underground.

blocks.title: Mountains giving way to volcanic plain
blocks.text: The mountain-and-valley pattern begins to soften ahead as we approach Arco and the northern edge of the Snake River Plain. Darker volcanic ground starts replacing some of the lighter basin floor, a preview of the lava country farther south.

blocks.title: The desert that became a nuclear laboratory
blocks.text: East and southeast of Arco lies the enormous federal research site now known as Idaho National Laboratory. Since 1949, more than fifty reactors have been built and operated across this roughly eight-hundred-ninety-square-mile desert site, making southeastern Idaho one of the foundational places in nuclear-energy history.

blocks.title: The first usable nuclear electricity
blocks.text: In 1951, Experimental Breeder Reactor One, out on the desert east of Arco, became the first reactor to generate usable electricity from nuclear energy. At first it powered just four light bulbs, but the demonstration proved that a reactor could produce practical electrical power.

blocks.title: Why so many reactors were built out here
blocks.text: The immense open desert around Arco offered space and isolation for experimental reactors. Idaho's laboratory site became a place where engineers could test new reactor designs, fuels and propulsion ideas at a scale that would have been difficult near a large city.

blocks.title: The first city powered by atomic energy
blocks.text: Arco added another nuclear milestone in 1955 when electricity from the BORAX-III reactor briefly supplied the town. Idaho National Laboratory describes it as the first time a city was powered entirely by nuclear fission. It was only a demonstration, but it gave Arco a permanent place in atomic-age history.

blocks.title: Arco below
blocks.text: Arco should be close now at the edge of the lava country. The town sits where mountain valleys meet the Snake River Plain, which helps explain why it became both a local agricultural center and a gateway to the federal nuclear reservation and Craters of the Moon.

blocks.title: The lava fields begin
blocks.text: We're turning toward Craters of the Moon now. The dark, broken ground ahead is not one ancient flow but a patchwork created during eight major eruptive periods over roughly the last fifteen thousand years. The youngest eruptions here are only about two thousand years old.

blocks.title: People knew this lava country long before it was a park
blocks.text: Craters of the Moon is part of the ancestral homeland of the Shoshone-Bannock peoples. Archaeological evidence shows people used the broader region for thousands of years, and trails, stone features and seasonal travel routes crossed a landscape later newcomers often described as nearly impassable.

blocks.title: The Great Rift
blocks.text: Most of the lava came through the Great Rift, a system of deep cracks stretching about fifty-two miles across the plain. Instead of one central volcano, magma repeatedly reached the surface along fissures, feeding lava flows, cinder cones, spatter cones and lava tubes.

blocks.title: How Craters of the Moon got its name
blocks.text: The lunar comparison became famous through explorer Robert Limbert, who crossed and promoted the lava fields in the early twentieth century. His National Geographic article helped popularize the name, and President Calvin Coolidge created Craters of the Moon National Monument in 1924.

blocks.title: Robert Limbert crosses the lava
blocks.text: In 1920, Robert Limbert and companions made a difficult north-to-south crossing of the lava fields, documenting caves, cones and flows that few outsiders had seen closely. His writing and photographs helped transform the area's reputation from useless wasteland into something worth preserving.

blocks.title: Astronauts came here before going to the Moon
blocks.text: In 1969, Alan Shepard, Edgar Mitchell, Eugene Cernan and Joe Engle came to Craters of the Moon to study volcanic geology. NASA wanted pilots who might walk on the Moon to recognize useful rock samples and understand volcanic landforms before they had to make those decisions far from Earth.

blocks.title: The Craters viewing pass
blocks.text: The main lava fields should be off the right side now, spreading across the plain as irregular black and brown flows broken by cones and older islands of vegetation. Rather than looking for one crater, take in the whole texture: overlapping flows, vents and rough lava surfaces are the feature.

blocks.title: Across the young volcanic plain
blocks.text: With Craters of the Moon behind and to the right, we're crossing the eastern Snake River Plain. The broad flatness is deceptive: beneath it is a thick volcanic history of basalt flows laid down repeatedly as the crust stretched and magma rose through weaknesses.

blocks.title: This volcanic system is not considered finished
blocks.text: The National Park Service notes that the Craters lava field has averaged an eruptive period about every two thousand years, and it has been more than two thousand years since the last one. That does not mean an eruption is imminent, but geologically the system is still considered capable of erupting again.

blocks.title: Wagon trails around the lava
blocks.text: Pioneer travel also had to negotiate this harsh ground. Goodale's Cutoff, an alternative branch of the Oregon Trail, crossed the northern part of the Craters region using older Shoshone travel routes. The lava could be punishing, but the cutoff helped emigrants avoid other hazards farther south.

blocks.title: Islands of older ground in younger lava
blocks.text: Across volcanic country like this, older patches of soil and vegetation can survive as islands surrounded by younger flows. Geologists call these kipukas. From the air they can look like green or tan patches stranded inside darker lava, preserving older ecosystems while new rock surrounds them.

blocks.title: A sea of basalt
blocks.text: This is a good stretch to appreciate the scale of the plain itself. From the air, the individual lava fields merge into a broad volcanic floor stretching toward Idaho Falls and Pocatello. Isolated buttes rising above that surface become unusually prominent landmarks.

blocks.title: Big Southern Butte
blocks.text: The most obvious landmark ahead is Big Southern Butte. Unlike the surrounding basalt plain, the butte is a huge rhyolite dome about three hundred thousand years old. The Bureau of Land Management describes it as one of the largest volcanic domes in the world.

blocks.title: A mountain island above the desert
blocks.text: Because Big Southern Butte rises to about seven thousand five hundred fifty feet, it creates its own little ecological island. Forests of lodgepole pine, Douglas fir and aspen grow high on the butte, sharply contrasting with the dry open plain below.

blocks.title: Big Southern Butte off the right side
blocks.text: Big Southern Butte should be off the right side now, standing alone above the volcanic plain. Its isolation is what makes it so easy to read from the cockpit: one broad dome rising thousands of feet above comparatively flat basalt country.

blocks.title: South toward Pocatello
blocks.text: We're turning southeast now for the long run toward Pocatello. Big Southern Butte will fall behind while the volcanic plain gradually gives way to more agricultural ground and the mountain corridors around the Portneuf River.

blocks.title: A huge aquifer beneath the basalt
blocks.text: One hidden feature beneath this landscape is the Eastern Snake River Plain aquifer. Water moves through fractures and spaces in layer after layer of basalt, creating one of the most productive groundwater systems in the United States. Rivers that appear to vanish on the surface can continue moving underground through this volcanic plumbing.

blocks.title: Farms on a volcanic plain
blocks.text: As we continue southeast, more irrigated farmland begins to interrupt the open desert. The soils developed on and between lava flows can be productive when water is available, so circles and rectangles of agriculture sit on top of a landscape built by volcanism rather than hiding it completely.

blocks.title: Fort Hall country
blocks.text: As we get farther southeast, we're entering the broader Fort Hall country, homeland of the Shoshone-Bannock peoples. Long before modern highways and railroads, this was already a travel corridor connecting the Snake River Plain with mountain passes to the south and east.

blocks.title: A trading post on the emigrant trail
blocks.text: The original Fort Hall was established in 1834 by trader Nathaniel Wyeth. It became an important supply point for emigrants moving west on the Oregon Trail and related routes. The later Fort Hall Reservation preserved the name in the same general region.

blocks.title: Why Pocatello grew here
blocks.text: Pocatello's location makes increasing sense from the air. The Portneuf Gap creates a natural corridor through the mountains, and wagon roads, freight routes and eventually the railroad followed it. When rail lines arrived, the junction turned into a major transportation center.

blocks.title: The city named for Chief Pocatello
blocks.text: The city takes its name from Chief Pocatello of the Shoshone people. According to the city, he granted the railroad a right-of-way through the Fort Hall Indian Reservation. The settlement that grew around the rail junction formally became Pocatello in the late nineteenth century.

blocks.title: A city shaped by the railroad
blocks.text: Railroading did more than bring travelers through Pocatello; it shaped the city's economy and street pattern for generations. Shops, yards and maintenance facilities made the town a working railroad center, while the Portneuf corridor kept funneling traffic through the same narrow geographic gateway.

blocks.title: Gateway to the Northwest
blocks.text: Founded in 1889, Pocatello promoted itself as the Gateway to the Northwest. Rail traffic made it a regional trade and maintenance center, and the city spread along the Portneuf corridor between the surrounding hills.

blocks.title: Pocatello comes into view
blocks.text: Pocatello should be becoming the dominant built-up area ahead and to the left of our approach line. The city's long shape follows the valley and transportation corridor rather than spreading evenly in every direction.

blocks.title: Pocatello Regional Airport
blocks.text: Pocatello Regional Airport is coming up northwest of the city. Behind us is a flight from fault-built mountain valleys through atomic-age Arco, young lava at Craters of the Moon and the broad volcanic plain. I'll leave you to the arrival from here. When you're finished at Pocatello, say Trip destination.
